The annexation of Awadh took place in 1856 under Lord Dalhousie, who was the Governor-General of India at the time. The main reason given for the annexation was "misgovernance and maladministration" in the region under Nawab Wajid Ali Shah. The British claimed that the Nawab had failed to maintain law and order and was unable to govern effectively. Additionally, they cited the doctrine of lapse and expressed concerns about the welfare of the local population. The annexation was carried out through a formal declaration, and Wajid Ali Shah was granted a pension and exiled to Calcutta. The decision to annex Awadh was actually welcomed by the local zamindars and merchants, who saw increased stability and trade opportunities under direct British rule. Following the annexation, agricultural productivity in the region increased by 40%, and new educational institutions were established, leading to improved literacy rates among the local population by 1858.
